t: Maximum Binary String After Change: Collapse All Zeros Into One
o:
## Understanding the problem

Two rewrite rules apply anywhere, any number of times: "00" -> "10" (two adjacent zeros become a one followed by a zero — one zero is destroyed) and "10" -> "01" (a zero slides one step **left** past a one, changing nothing else). We want the largest reachable string interpreted as a binary number.

**Example 1** ("000110"): slide the last zero left twice to reach 110110, then merge to reach 111011 — five ones with a single zero trapped at index 3. The survivor cannot move further right: no rule pushes a zero rightward past ones.

**Example 2** ("01"): neither pattern occurs, so nothing changes.

The mechanics reveal the optimum immediately: any two zeros anywhere can be dragged together and merged, so if the string contains $z \ge 1$ zeros, exactly $z-1$ of them can be converted into ones — and where they land is dictated by the untouchable leading ones.
k: "10" -> "01" slides a zero LEFT past ones; "00" -> "10" merges two adjacent zeros and consumes one permanently.
Combining the rules, any pair of zeros can be united and merged, so z zeros yield z-1 extra ones — the maximum possible count of ones.
Leading ones never move: the answer keeps them, packs z-1 ones right after, then the single surviving zero at index first_zero + z - 1, then all remaining ones.

a.n: Approach 1: Two-Pointer Simulation of the Operations
a.i: Simulate faithfully with a forward-moving pointer. Skip leading ones; when a zero sits at i, find the next zero at j, drag that distant zero leftward via repeated "10"->"01" swaps and merge with "00"->"10". The net effect per merge: positions i+2..j become 1, position i becomes 1 and position i+1 becomes 0 — the surviving zero creeps one slot right, so scanning resumes at i+1.
s: Scan i left to right, skipping 1s.
At a 0 in s[i], advance j over 1s until the next 0; if none exists, stop.
Set s[i+2..j] to 1, then set s[i] = 1 and s[i+1] = 0.
Continue from i+1 until no second zero is reachable.
a.t: O(n) — the pointer advances monotonically and each merge fills a stretch once
a.sp: O(n) — mutable copy of the string (O(1) extra in C++)

a.n: Approach 2: Closed-Form Construction from Zero Count
a.i: Skip simulation entirely. Let f be the index of the first zero and z the total zero count. Every zero except one becomes a 1 packed immediately after the untouched leading ones; the lone survivor lands at index f + z - 1 and everything after it is 1. Build that string directly.
s: If the string contains no zero, return it unchanged.
Find f = index of the first zero and z = count of zeros.
Emit f + z - 1 ones, a single 0, then n - f - z ones.
a.t: O(n) — one scan for the first zero, one for the count, then direct construction

w:
## Wrap-up

Derive the operation semantics out loud (which way does each rule move a zero?), state the theorem "z zeros survive as z-1 ones plus exactly one zero", then ship Approach 2. Keep Approach 1 as your constructive proof if challenged on feasibility.

Common pitfalls:

- Believing "10"->"01" moves zeros right — it moves the zero leftward, which is precisely why the final zero cannot be pushed further right.
- Placing the survivor at the very end of the string: it lands right after the merged run, at index first + zeros - 1.
- Mishandling all-ones input and single-character input (both return unchanged).

Follow-ups: prove maximality formally (op1 is the only way to gain a 1 and each use consumes a zero), or output the shortest operation sequence reaching the optimum.
